translation: The most important thing that happened to me in the winter of 1993 was my dad returning home, just one week before my mom got married.
One afternoon in December, he came to the school looking for me.
I ran all the way to the gate, and through the iron bars I could see him standing outside, smoking a cigarette from afar.
Wearing a long black trench coat, the upright collar covering half of the face.
I don't know why, but without even getting a clear look at him, I feel as though he is not doing well.
My heart ached, and tears fell from my eyes.
I never thought that my mother would consider remarrying.
Perhaps subconsciously, I felt she should continue to suffer because of my father's departure, just like me.
Moreover, I feel that she lacks the ability to find happiness.
Perhaps it's true, but happiness has the ability to find her.
Isn't it so?
As a beauty, she doesn't need to work that hard.
She doesn't need to do anything.
All she needs to do is stand in her place.
I still remember, that year the winter was particularly long, half of April had passed and the winter jasmine had not yet bloomed.
The divorce of your parents has left you feeling very depressed.
We haven't had any new games for a long time and would aimlessly sit on the roof of the dead man's tower every evening.
Among the body parts scattered in the yard, a few more arms had appeared.
We used hooks to gather them together, arranging them into a Thousand-Hand Guanyin.
My father actually knew nothing about doing business, he just went to join a distant cousin who he was not familiar with.
My grandmother had a sister who went to Beijing at a young age and later got married and had children there.
This cousin was the eldest son of her family and had always been considered as an outsider among the entire family.
Just now you said that everyone has a time when their luck begins, as if life has suddenly been reigned in.
I must have been eight years old.
That autumn, my father left Jinan and went to Beijing alone.
Since then, I no longer had a home.
I don't intend to keep the appointment.
No matter the reason, I think there's no need for us to meet again.
I sat on the couch, chain-smoking.
As it was getting darker, there was a sudden knock at the door.
Deliver
The boy of the water stood at the door with a bucket, saying he was going to deliver water to a family in the western suburbs.
He wore a dirty, grey woolen hat, with a vacant expression on his face.
Our conversation was very difficult.
Every time I fell silent, my heart would feel constricted.
All I wanted was to end this meeting quickly.
You seem to notice something, but are still trying hard to find a topic.
The tea has cooled, the white fog in the room has dissipated, and finally, you rise to take your leave.
Just as I closed the door and let out a sigh of relief, the doorbell rang again.
You stood at the doorway, asking me to come to the small white building later.
Before I had time to decline, you had already walked out of the building.
I went into the kitchen to turn off the stove.
Half of the water in the pot had evaporated, filling the room with a white mist.
You sat uncomfortably, watching me pour tea.
"Do you still live with your grandmother and aunt?"
You ask.
I'm telling you, my grandmother has passed away and now I live with my aunt.
"She never settled down," you ask.
"Hmm.

The white breath coming from your lips, curly hair rustled by the wind, and the subtle shiver of your knees under your coat's hemline all convince me that you standing here are real, not an extension of a previous dream.
It's been eighteen years, so it's not surprising if you don't recognize me.
You didn't wear any make-up, your pale face was a bit swollen, but at least you didn't let everyone down; you grew into a beauty.
Only, her small peachy face was gloomy, bearing the look of one who had been in the big city for too long.
You ask me if you look different than what I had imagined.
I smiled noncommittally.
Frankly, I've never imagined what you would look like when you grow up.
As far as I'm concerned, everything related to you has already been put into a file bag and marked with a seal.
It may hurt to say this, but honestly, I don't look forward to seeing you again.
I open my eyes.
You are standing at the doorway.
I have no idea how long you have been standing there, you probably even saw me laughing in my dreams.
And the sadness upon waking, looking your weakest.
Cheng Gong, you whispered my name in a hoarse voice, as if you hadn't spoken in a very long time.
It was about to snow, the sky was terribly overcast, and the house was pitch black.
The water in the pot was boiling, bubbling and rolling over.
I looked at you closely for a while, certain that I did not know you.
But in the dim light, I suddenly felt a deep connection with this stranger standing opposite me.
That feeling sent chills down my spine.
I tried to recall, the cards of memory fluttering in my mind.
And then you said, "You are Li Jiaqi.
